p.x:
Songkran is the Thai New Year festival. People celebrate it from the 13th to the 15th of April, the hottest time of the year. It is a special time for families. Many people who work in Bangkok travel back to their home towns to see their parents and grandparents.
On the first morning, families often go to the temple to give food to the monks. Then young people pour water on the hands of older people to show respect and to wish them good luck. This is an old tradition.
In the afternoon, the fun begins! People of all ages throw water at each other in the streets. In some towns there is a parade, with music, dancing and people in traditional costumes. Tourists love to join in, and many hotels invite their guests to a Songkran party. Just remember: if you go out, you will get very wet!

Loy Krathong is one of Thailand's most beautiful occasions. It takes place on the night of the full moon in the twelfth month of the Thai lunar calendar, usually in November. People make a krathong, a small boat made from banana leaves, decorated with flowers, a candle and incense, and float it on a river or lake.
The custom has several meanings. One popular belief is that it is a way to say thank you to the water goddess and to show respect for the water that gives us life. Others see it as a way to let go of bad luck and anger from the past year. Some families also remember their ancestors on this night.
In Chiang Mai, the festival is combined with Yi Peng, when thousands of paper lanterns rise into the sky. There is also a religious ceremony at some temples, led by monks. The crowds can be enormous, so it's best to arrive early. In recent years, many cities have encouraged people to use bread or other natural materials instead of plastic foam, because the old type of krathong polluted the rivers.

Every culture has festivals that commemorate important events, from harvests to historical victories. Many of these celebrations are part of a community's intangible heritage: they are not buildings or objects, but practices passed down through generations. A ritual such as making an offering of food at a shrine, or walking in a candlelit procession around a temple, connects people to their ancestors and to each other.
In Thailand, festivals are closely linked to Buddhist ideas. Devotees visit temples to make merit, hoping to improve their lives in this world and the next. Colours, flowers and numbers often symbolise good fortune, and many families still consult monks to choose an auspicious date for important events. Alongside religion, local folklore adds colour: stories of spirits, magical animals and heroes are retold every year.
Yet many people worry that festivals are becoming commercialised. Shopping malls run Songkran promotions, brands sponsor parades, and some traditions are performed mainly for tourists' cameras. Defenders reply that traditions have always changed, and that tourism brings money that helps communities preserve their culture. The real question may be whether people still understand the meaning behind the celebration.
